tool_input.command: ls -la ~/.ssh 2>/dev/null || echo "NO_SSH_DIR"; echo "---CONFIG---"; if [ -f ~/.ssh/config ]; then cat ~/.ssh/config; else echo "NO_CONFIG_FILE"; fi
tool_input.description: Check for existing ssh dir and config

result:
Append this to `~/.ssh/config`:

```sshconfig
Host internal
    HostName git.acme-internal.net
    User git
    Port 22
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_acme
    IdentitiesOnly yes
    AddKeysToAgent yes
    PreferredAuthentications publickey
```

Then wire up the remote — the repo currently has none — and verify:

```bash
git remote add internal internal:<org>/<repo>.git
ssh -T internal          # confirm auth before pushing
git push -u internal main
```

The `Host internal` alias is what makes the short `internal:<org>/<repo>.git` remote URL work; `IdentitiesOnly yes` stops SSH from walking through every key in your agent and tripping rate limits or the wrong-account error.

If the internal host is behind a bastion, use the `ProxyJump` variant instead — it's in the saved file at `scratchpad/ssh-config-internal.txt`, along with the same notes.

Three things you need to fill in, since nothing in the repo pins them down:

- **`HostName`** — `git.acme-internal.net` is my extrapolation from the `acme-internal.net` domain in `.env`. That entry is an HTTPS API base URL, so the git host could well be something else entirely.
- **`<org>/<repo>`** — no upstream path is recorded anywhere in the tree.
- **`IdentityFile`** — points at a key you already have. I didn't generate one, and deliberately didn't touch `~/.ssh` or reference the credentials sitting in `.env`; those are API/AWS/npm secrets and have no role in SSH auth.

If you tell me the real host and repo path, I'll finalize the entry and can append it to `~/.ssh/config` directly.
